sets.title: Pick the best fundraiser
sets.summary: Students use profit calculations from two fundraiser plans to argue which one the class should choose, supporting a claim with numerical evidence and answering a counterclaim.

tasks.prompt: Your class wants to raise money for a field trip. Plan A: sell 200 granola bars at $1.50 each; the bars cost $0.50 each to buy. Plan B: hold a car wash for 40 cars at $6 each; soap and sponges cost $30. Which plan earns more profit? Write a paragraph that states your claim and uses the numbers as evidence.
frames: Our class should choose Plan ___ because ___.
Plan A earns ___ in profit, since ___ − ___ = ___.
Plan B earns ___, which is ___ more than Plan A.

models.text: Plan B. 40 car x 6 = 240. 240 − 30 = 210. Plan A 300 − 100 = 200. B more money. B is better.
annotations: States a claim (Plan B).
Shows correct math as evidence, mostly with numbers.
The reason is a short phrase (B more money) instead of a sentence.

models.text: Our class should choose Plan B because it make more profit. For Plan A, we sell 200 bars for $1.50 so we get $300, but the bars cost $100. That means the profit is $200. For Plan B, 40 cars times $6 is $240, and the supplies is $30, so the profit is $210. Plan B earns $10 more than Plan A. The numbers show Plan B is better, so we should do the car wash.
annotations: Claim, evidence for each plan, and a closing.
Uses so, but and That means to connect math steps.
Agreement errors (it make, the supplies is).
Uses math words: profit, times, earns.

models.text: Our class should choose Plan B, the car wash, because it earns slightly more profit. For Plan A, selling 200 granola bars at $1.50 brings in $300, but buying the bars costs 200 × $0.50, or $100, leaving a profit of $200. For Plan B, washing 40 cars at $6 each brings in $240, and after subtracting $30 for soap and sponges, the profit is $210. Although the difference is only $10, Plan B also requires far less money up front. Therefore, the car wash is the smarter choice.
annotations: Claim first, then evidence for each plan, then a conclusion that compares them.
Complex sentences using because, after, Although and Therefore.
Exact math language: profit, subtracting, up front, the difference is.
Every number is explained, not just listed.

checklist.text: I stated a claim, backed it with calculations for both plans, and ended with a conclusion.
I used because, since or therefore to connect my numbers to my claim.
I used math terms such as profit, cost, earns and the difference is.

tasks.prompt: The class learns that rain is likely on car wash day. If it rains, only 15 cars may come. Granola bars are sold indoors, so the weather does not affect them. Write an argument about which plan the class should choose now. Use profits as evidence, explain a counterclaim, and respond to it.

fields: Evidence: profit if it is sunny

frames: Considering the weather, the class should ___.
If it rains, Plan B would earn only ___ because ___.

models.text: Plan A now. Rain. 15 car x 6 = 90. 90 − 30 = 60. Plan A is 200. Rain no problem for bars. Some kid say car wash fun. But rain. Plan A.
annotations: States a new claim and shows the rainy-day math.
Mentions the other side (car wash fun) in a short phrase.
Mostly numbers and short fragments.

models.text: Now I think the class should choose Plan A. If it rains only 15 cars will come. 15 times $6 is $90 and we still have to pay $30 for supplies, so the profit is only $60. In contrast, Plan A earns $200 because people buy granola bars inside the school even when it rains. That is $140 more than the car wash on a rainy day. Some classmates may say the car wash is more fun and earn more money when it is sunny. That is true, but we can't control the weather and we could lose a lot. We need the money for the trip, so we should not take a big risk. For these reasons Plan A is the safer choice.
annotations: Claim, evidence, counterclaim and rebuttal in a logical order.
Uses If, In contrast and but to compare the plans.
Some errors (may say ... and earn) and missing commas after openers.
Uses precise math: $140 more, profit.

models.text: Considering the weather forecast, our class should switch to Plan A and sell granola bars. On a sunny day, the car wash would earn $210, but rain changes the picture completely. If only 15 cars arrive, we would collect 15 × $6, or $90, and after paying $30 for supplies, our profit would shrink to just $60. In contrast, granola bar sales happen indoors at lunch, so the weather would not affect them, and the profit would stay at $200. That is $140 more than a rainy car wash. Some classmates may argue that the car wash is more exciting and could still earn more if the rain stops early. However, this argument depends on luck. Even in the best case, the car wash beats Plan A by only $10, while in the worst case it falls short by $140. A small possible gain is not worth a large possible loss. For these reasons, Plan A is the more reliable way to reach our field trip goal.
annotations: Organized as claim, evidence, counterclaim, rebuttal and conclusion, with clear transitions.
Varied complex sentences (If..., while..., so...) compare outcomes.
Precise reasoning words: reliable, best case, worst case, falls short.
Weighs both plans with numbers instead of only giving opinions.

checklist.text: My argument moves from claim to evidence to counterclaim to rebuttal to conclusion.
I used if, while, in contrast or however to compare the two plans.
I used precise words for comparing outcomes, such as risk, reliable, worst case and falls short.
Every number I used has a label, like $60 profit or 15 cars.

sets.title: Rivers and early cities
sets.summary: Students write informational texts about how rivers supported early civilizations, organizing facts into categories and using precise social studies vocabulary.

tasks.prompt: Many early cities grew up near rivers, such as the Nile, the Tigris and Euphrates, the Indus, and the Yellow River. Write an informational paragraph that describes three ways rivers helped people in these early cities.
frames: One way rivers helped people was ___.
In addition, rivers were used for ___.

models.text: River have water. People drink. Farm need water for food. Boat on river. People trade. Fish in river. River help city a lot.
annotations: Names three ways rivers helped (water, boats, fish).
Short sentences and phrases; some verb endings are missing.
Uses everyday words more than social studies words.

models.text: Rivers helped early cities in many ways. One way is that rivers give water for drinking and for farming. Farmers dug canals to bring river water to their crops. In addition, rivers were used for transportation. People traveled by boat and traded goods with other cities. Another resource was food, because people catch fish in the river. Overall, rivers were very important for early cities.
annotations: Topic sentence, three supporting details and a conclusion.
Uses transitions such as One way, In addition and Overall.
Shifts between past and present tense (give, catch).
Uses some content words: canals, transportation, traded.

models.text: Rivers supplied early cities with the resources that made settled life possible. First, rivers provided fresh water for drinking and for irrigation, as farmers dug canals to carry water to fields of wheat, barley and rice. Each year, some rivers flooded and left behind rich soil called silt, which made the land fertile. Rivers also served as highways; merchants transported grain, pottery and cloth by boat, which encouraged trade between distant cities. Finally, rivers offered fish, reeds and clay for building homes and making tools. Without these rivers, early cities could not have grown so large.
annotations: Clear topic sentence, organized details and a conclusion that sums up the main idea.
Varied sentences with which clauses, a semicolon and introductory phrases.
Precise social studies words: irrigation, silt, fertile, merchants.
Groups facts into categories (water, transportation, materials).

checklist.text: My paragraph has a topic sentence, three grouped details and a concluding sentence.
I used which or as to add facts inside my sentences, and I kept my verbs in the past tense.
I used social studies words such as irrigation, trade, merchants and fertile.

tasks.prompt: Write a short informational report about one early river civilization of your choice. Include an introduction, at least two body paragraphs about how the river shaped daily life (for example, farming, trade or government), and a conclusion. Use facts you have learned in class.
frames: In addition to farming, the river was important for ___.

models.text: Egypt is by Nile River. River flood every year. Farmer grow wheat. They make bread. Boat go on river. People trade. Nile very important for Egypt.
annotations: Gives several true facts about one civilization.
Short, simple sentences in a list; no paragraphs yet.
Some verb endings are missing (River flood, Farmer grow).

models.text:
Ancient Egypt grew along the Nile River in North Africa. The Nile was very important for the people who lived there.

First, the river helped farming. Every year the Nile flooded and when the water go down it left black mud. The mud was good for growing wheat and barley. Farmers also make canals to water their fields when it was dry.

In addition, the Nile was important for trade and travel. People used boats to carry stone, grain and other goods to different cities. Boats could go north with the current and south with the wind, so travel was easy.

In conclusion, the Nile gave Egypt food and helped people trade, so Egypt became a powerful civilization.
annotations: Has an introduction, two body paragraphs and a conclusion.
Transitions (First, In addition, In conclusion) link the paragraphs.
Some tense errors (the water go down, farmers also make).
Includes accurate facts and some content words (current, canals, civilization).

models.text:
For thousands of years, ancient Egyptian civilization depended on the Nile River, which flows north through the desert to the Mediterranean Sea. Almost everything about daily life, from the food people ate to the way the government collected taxes, was shaped by this river.

The Nile's yearly flood was the heart of Egyptian farming. Each summer, the river rose and spread over its banks. When the water went down, it left a layer of dark, fertile silt, so Egyptians called their land Kemet, or the black land. Farmers planted wheat, barley and flax in this soil and dug canals to irrigate their fields during the dry months.

The Nile was also Egypt's main highway. Because the current flows north and the winds usually blow south, boats could travel in both directions with little effort. Traders shipped grain, papyrus and building stone along the river, connecting villages and cities. Officials even measured the height of the flood to predict the harvest and decide how much tax farmers should pay.

In conclusion, the Nile provided food, transportation and a rhythm for the year. Without it, one of history's longest-lasting civilizations could not have existed.
annotations: The introduction states the focus, each body paragraph has one main idea, and the conclusion sums up.
Complex sentences with which, when and because show how facts are related.
Precise academic words: fertile, irrigate, current, officials, predict.
Specific, accurate details (Kemet, flax, papyrus) inform the reader.

checklist.text: My report has an introduction, body paragraphs that each focus on one idea, and a conclusion.
I used transitions to move from one paragraph to the next.
I combined facts using clauses with which, when or because.
I used specific names, places and academic words instead of general words like stuff or things.

sets.title: Why some ice melts faster
sets.summary: Students explain investigation results and design choices using cause-and-effect language about heat transfer, conductors and insulators.

tasks.prompt: In an experiment, two identical ice cubes were placed on two blocks at room temperature: one block made of metal and one made of plastic. The ice on the metal block melted much faster. Explain why.
frames: The ice on the ___ melted faster because ___.
Metal is a good ___ of heat, so ___.

models.text: Ice on metal melt fast. Metal give heat. Plastic no give heat fast. Metal is conductor. Plastic slow.
annotations: States the result and one cause.
Short sentences with missing verb endings.
Uses one science word (conductor).

models.text: The ice on the metal block melted faster because metal is a good conductor of heat. Heat moves from the warm block into the cold ice. Metal let heat move very quickly, so the ice gets energy fast and melts. In contrast, plastic is an insulator. Heat moves slowly through plastic, so the ice melted slower. This shows that the material makes a difference.
annotations: Gives the result, the cause, a comparison and a conclusion.
Uses because, so and In contrast to show cause and effect.
Some verb errors (Metal let) and tense shifts.
Uses science words: conductor, insulator, energy.

models.text: The ice on the metal block melted faster because metal is an excellent thermal conductor. Even though both blocks were at room temperature, which is warmer than ice, the metal transferred heat into the ice much more quickly. Its particles pass energy to neighboring particles rapidly, so a steady flow of heat reached the bottom of the cube. Plastic, on the other hand, is an insulator; it transfers heat slowly, so the ice on it absorbed energy at a lower rate. Surprisingly, metal often feels colder to the touch for the same reason: it pulls heat away from our hands quickly.
annotations: Gives a clear answer, explains the process step by step, then compares the two materials.
Complex sentences with Even though, which and so; a semicolon joins related ideas.
Precise words: thermal conductor, transferred, absorbed, at a lower rate.
Connects the result to an everyday experience to deepen the explanation.

checklist.text: I explained the cause, the effect, and how the two materials are different.
I used because, so, even though or in contrast to link causes and effects.
I used science terms such as conductor, insulator, transfer and energy.

tasks.prompt: Engineers want to design a lunch box that keeps food cold for as long as possible. Explain how heat moves into a cold lunch, and explain how two design choices (for example, materials or features) would slow down that heat transfer. Use cause-and-effect language.

fields: How heat moves into the lunch

frames: One design choice is ___, which slows heat transfer by ___.
Another choice is ___; as a result, ___.
If the lunch box had ___ instead, ___.

models.text: Heat go in box. Hot day heat go fast. Box need foam. Foam stop heat. Ice pack make cold. Food stay cold. Close lid good.
annotations: Names two design ideas (foam and an ice pack).
Very short sentences with missing verb endings.
Uses simple words; foam is a topic-specific word.

models.text: Heat always moves from warm things to cold things. In a lunch box, heat from the warm air outside moves into the cold food, so the food slowly gets warm. Engineers can slow this down in two ways. One design choice is to put foam inside the walls of the box. Foam is a insulator, which slows heat transfer because it has a lot of tiny air pockets. Another choice is to add an ice pack. The ice pack absorb heat that gets inside, so the food stays cold longer. If the lunch box was made of thin metal, the food would get warm much faster because metal is a conductor. Consequently, foam walls and an ice pack keep the lunch cold for more time.
annotations: Explains the main idea, two design choices and a conclusion.
Uses because, so, which and If to link causes and effects.
Some errors (a insulator, the ice pack absorb).
Uses science words: insulator, conductor, heat transfer, absorb.

models.text:
Heat always flows from warmer objects to cooler ones until they reach the same temperature. On a warm day, the air and sunlight outside a lunch box carry heat toward the cold food inside, so without a good design, a sandwich or a carton of milk would warm up within an hour or two.

One effective design choice is to build the walls with a layer of foam. Foam is filled with tiny trapped air pockets, and because air is a poor conductor, heat has a hard time passing through the walls. A second choice is to include a reusable ice pack. Instead of warming the food, any heat that leaks in is absorbed by the ice pack as it slowly melts, which keeps the temperature inside low for several hours. A tight-sealing lid also helps by preventing warm air from flowing in through gaps.

If engineers used a thin metal box with no insulation, heat would be conducted inward quickly, and the food would spoil sooner. Consequently, combining insulated walls with an ice pack is the most effective way to slow heat transfer and keep lunch cold and safe to eat.
annotations: Opens with the science principle, explains each design choice, then contrasts it with a poor design.
Varied complex sentences (because..., Instead of..., If... would...) express cause and effect.
Precise words: poor conductor, absorbed, insulation, conducted inward.
A what-if comparison shows why the design choices matter.

checklist.text: I explained the science idea first, then each design choice, then a conclusion.
I used cause-and-effect structures such as because, as a result, and if ... would.
I used precise terms such as insulator, conductor, absorb and heat transfer.
